source.title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source.publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

types_covered: Secondary headache due to serious underlying conditions

sections.label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
items: The worst headache of your life, a sudden, extremely severe headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to minutes (thunderclap headache). This can be a sign of bleeding in the brain.
First ever severe headache, especially in a person who does not usually get headaches
Headache with fever and stiff neck, may indicate meningitis
Headache with fever and change in behaviour, personality, or level of consciousness
Headache with confusion or disorientation
Headache with weakness, numbness, or paralysis on one side of the body or face
Headache with sudden vision changes or vision loss
Severe headache that wakes you up from sleep
Headache in a pregnant woman or someone who has recently given birth
New headache type in a person with cancer or a weakened immune system
Progressive headache that is steadily getting worse over days or weeks
Headache associated with a recent head injury

sections.label: Self-Care for Common Tension Headache or Known Migraine
items: Rest in a quiet, dark, and cool room, this is especially helpful for migraine
Paracetamol can be taken for pain relief as per the dosage on the pack
Stay hydrated, dehydration is a common trigger for headaches
Apply a cold or warm compress to the forehead or the back of the neck
Avoid known personal triggers: irregular sleep, skipping meals, too much screen time, bright lights, strong smells, stress
Ensure at least 6 hours of sleep regularly, sleep deprivation is a major trigger for both tension headache and migraine
Reduce caffeine intake gradually if you consume large amounts, sudden stopping can also trigger headaches
Stress management: take short breaks, practice deep breathing, and avoid overwork
For migraine, lie down in a dark room and sleep if possible, sleep often relieves migraine
Do not take painkillers more than 3 days a week for headaches, overuse of painkillers causes its own rebound headaches

sections.label: See a Doctor
items: Headaches occurring more than twice a month
Headaches that are interfering with daily work or sleep
Headaches that are getting more frequent or more severe over time
Migraine not responding to paracetamol
Headache always on the same side of the head
Headache with nausea and vomiting regularly
Tension headache persisting for many years with significant sleep disturbance
Any new or unusual headache pattern that you have not had before

sections.label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
items: Any red flag sign listed above, thunderclap headache, fever with stiff neck, confusion, one-sided weakness, vision loss, worst headache of your life
Headache that is progressively worsening over days and not responding to any treatment
Headache with seizures or loss of consciousness
Headache in someone with a known cancer or on immunosuppressive drugs
Severe migraine with hemiplegia (arm or leg weakness on one side), vertigo, or significant visual impairment, these are atypical and need urgent evaluation to rule out stroke

review.notes: All drug names and dosing excluded, including paracetamol dosing for migraine (listed in source). Retained paracetamol as a named option only in self-care because it is available OTC and the instruction to use it as labelled is safe. Red flag signs retained in full, these are the most clinically critical content in this document and map directly to the emergency and refer rules.
